def: A count of floating-point operations (additions or multiplications), the amount of arithmetic a computation needs, as distinct from FLOP/s, the speed at which hardware performs it.
The estimate that training a dense Transformer on D tokens takes about 6 times its parameter count N times D floating-point operations: 2 per weight per token forward and 4 backward.
The fraction of a GPU's peak arithmetic speed that a training run converts into useful model FLOPs, typically 30 to 50 per cent in large runs.
The most floating-point operations per second a chip could perform if every arithmetic unit were busy, as quoted on its datasheet.
The per-parameter training state that must stay in memory: weights, gradients, a full-precision master copy and the optimiser's running averages.
The memory cost of mixed-precision training with AdamW: 2 for bf16 weights, 2 for gradients, 4 for the fp32 master copy and 4 each for Adam's two moments.
The intermediate tensors saved during the forward pass because the backward pass needs them, whose memory grows with batch size, sequence length and depth.
Also called gradient checkpointing: discarding most activations in the forward pass and recomputing them during the backward pass, trading about a third more compute for much less memory.
The number of sequences processed in one forward and backward pass, which sets activation memory.
Summing the gradients of several microbatches before one optimiser step, to train with a large batch without holding its activations at once.
The stored keys and values of earlier tokens that attention reads when generating the next token, costing 2 times layers times key/value heads times head width times bytes per token.
A model's parameter count without its token and position tables, the N that Kaplan et al. use and that 6ND is most accurate with.
